lessons.title: Backtesting Risk Parity Strategies: Common Mistakes That Inflate Returns

children.text: This course has taken a few shortcuts for the sake of clarity. Chapter 2's leverage case study scaled returns by a leverage multiple without always walking through what compounding does to that number. Chapter 2's lookback window comparison computed weights once per window rather than re-estimating them through time. Real backtests that make these same shortcuts, often without realizing it, routinely report double-digit returns for strategies that would have actually lost money. This lesson names each mistake precisely and shows, with numbers, how much damage each one does.
Look-Ahead Bias: Weights That Use Information From the Future

markDefs.definition: A backtesting error where a strategy's decisions use data that would not actually have been available at the time the decision was supposedly made.

children.text: in a risk parity backtest is computing volatility and correlation once, using the entire sample period, and applying those same weights retroactively across the whole backtest. If your dataset runs from 2021 to 2025 and you estimate volatility using all five years of it, then apply the resulting ERC weights to your simulated 2021 portfolio, you are making a 2021 allocation decision using 2025 information that did not exist yet.

The fix is a walk-forward, or rolling, re-estimation: at every rebalance date, recompute volatility and correlation using only the data available up to that date, solve for new ERC weights, and hold them until the next rebalance. This is more work than computing one set of weights and stretching it across the whole backtest, and it is the only version of the backtest that reflects what an investor could actually have done in real time.

body.text: Chapter 2's lookback-window case study computed three separate sets of weights, one each for a 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year window, but each one was still a single static snapshot. A genuine backtest re-estimates on a rolling basis continuously through the test period, not once at the start. Treat that chapter's comparison as showing how sensitive the weights are to window choice, not as a template for how to actually run a backtest.

children.text: Ignoring Leverage Financing Costs: The Single Biggest Inflator

Chapter 2 built the levered return formula: expected levered return equals the unlevered return plus (leverage minus 1) times the gap between the unlevered return and the financing rate. A backtest that skips the financing term entirely, and simply multiplies the unlevered return by the leverage multiple, produces a dramatically better-looking number than any of the financing-aware versions from that lesson.

body.text: A 24.2% headline versus a -5.0% realistic outcome, on the exact same portfolio and the exact same leverage multiple, purely from whether financing cost is deducted and which financing route is assumed. Many online claims that 'risk parity beats equity returns with less risk' are built on exactly this naive, financing-free scaling. Always ask, when you see a levered backtest, whether a financing cost was subtracted at all, and if so, whose financing cost.

children.text: Variance Drag: Why Average Return Isn't Compounded Return

Chapter 2 flagged this and moved on. Here is the actual mechanism. Every return figure used so far in this course has been an arithmetic, expected return. What an investor actually experiences over multiple periods is the compounded, geometric return, and geometric return is always lower than arithmetic return when there is any volatility at all, because a 20% loss needs a 25% gain just to get back to even, an asymmetry that compounding punishes every period.

body.caption: The standard approximation for variance drag. The gap between arithmetic and geometric return grows with the square of volatility, which matters enormously once leverage has scaled volatility up.
Variance drag at three volatility levels (illustrative)

cells: Levered further, to double Nifty's volatility
12.00% becomes 8.08%, nearly a third of the return gone

body.text: Doubling volatility from 14% to 28% did not double the drag, it roughly quadrupled it, from 0.98% to 3.92%, because drag scales with volatility squared. This is a structural reason leverage has diminishing, then negative, appeal past a certain point: the arithmetic return from leverage grows linearly with L, from the formula in chapter 2, but variance drag grows quadratically with L. Applied to the case study's own numbers, the institutional-financing levered portfolio's 11.58% arithmetic return becomes roughly 10.6% once compounding is accounted for, and this course never mentioned that haircut when the number first appeared.

children.text: Execution Timing Bias: Trading on Information You Didn't Have Yet

A subtler version of look-ahead bias shows up in execution timing. A naive backtest computes a rebalancing signal using a day's closing price and assumes the trade executes at that exact same closing price. In reality, by the time that closing price is known, the market for the day is over, so any real trade has to happen at the next available price, typically the following session's open or close. Backtests that skip this one-period lag are quietly assuming perfect, instantaneous execution at a price the strategy could not actually have traded at.

Chapter 2 showed that a 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year lookback window each produced slightly different ERC weights and a different portfolio volatility estimate. If you run all three through a backtest and then report only the window that produced the best historical Sharpe ratio, you have quietly fit your methodology to the past, the same estimation-error problem from chapter 1, now smuggled in through a design choice made after seeing the results rather than before. A more honest approach fixes the lookback window using reasoning that does not depend on backtested performance, such as a horizon that matches your actual rebalancing cadence, and reports how the strategy performs across a range of plausible windows, not just the best one.

This course has stuck to broad, index-level sleeves, Nifty 50, G-Secs, gold, which sidesteps survivorship bias almost entirely, since an index is defined by whatever constituents it holds at each point in time. The moment you extend factor risk parity from chapter 3 to a custom universe of individual NSE stocks, survivorship bias becomes a live risk again: testing only on companies that are still listed and liquid today silently excludes every company that delisted, merged, or went bankrupt along the way, which can meaningfully flatter a backtest's results.

body.code:
import numpy as np

def honest_backtest(returns_by_asset, window, rebalance_every, financing_rate, leverage):
    """
    returns_by_asset: array of shape (T, n_assets), daily simple returns
    window: lookback length used to re-estimate vol/corr at each rebalance
    rebalance_every: rebalance cadence in trading days
    financing_rate: annualized cost of the levered (L-1) portion
    leverage: the fixed leverage multiple applied to ERC weights
    """
    T, n = returns_by_asset.shape
    weights = np.full(n, 1 / n)
    port_returns = []

    for t in range(window, T):
        if (t - window) % rebalance_every == 0:
            # walk-forward: only data strictly before today
            hist = returns_by_asset[t - window:t]
            vol = hist.std(axis=0) * np.sqrt(252)
            corr = np.corrcoef(hist.T)
            cov = np.outer(vol, vol) * corr
            w = np.full(n, 1 / n)
            for _ in range(500):
                pv = np.sqrt(w @ cov @ w)
                rc = (w * (cov @ w)) / pv
                w = w * (1 / n / (rc / pv)) ** 0.5
                w = w / w.sum()
            weights = w

        # execution lag: trade using TODAY's weights on TOMORROW's return, not today's
        if t + 1 < T:
            daily_financing = financing_rate / 252
            r = leverage * (weights @ returns_by_asset[t + 1]) - (leverage - 1) * daily_financing
            port_returns.append(r)

    port_returns = np.array(port_returns)
    arithmetic_annual = port_returns.mean() * 252
    geometric_annual = np.prod(1 + port_returns) ** (252 / len(port_returns)) - 1
    return arithmetic_annual, geometric_annual

# Plug in your own real NSE, G-Sec, and gold ETF daily return series.
# This skeleton fixes all four mistakes from this lesson in one place:
# walk-forward re-estimation, an execution lag, and an honest arithmetic
# vs geometric comparison. Leverage financing is subtracted every single day,
# not applied once at the end.
body.caption: This is a template, not a finished backtester, real implementations need to handle transaction costs, weight drift between rebalances, and data gaps too. But it fixes the three mistakes from this lesson that are easiest to accidentally skip: look-ahead in weight estimation, look-ahead in execution timing, and unfinanced leverage.

body.title: Diagnosing a Suspiciously Good Backtest
body.scenario: A post on a trading forum claims a 3x-levered Nifty and G-Sec risk parity strategy delivered a 28% CAGR over the last five years, comfortably beating Nifty 50's own returns with lower drawdowns. The post includes a chart but no methodology notes.
body.prompt: List, in order of how much impact each one would likely have, the questions you would ask before trusting this 28% figure.
body.modelAnswer: In rough order of likely impact: first, was any financing cost subtracted for the 3x leverage, and if so, whose rate, since this lesson showed the same portfolio can range from roughly -5% to +24% depending purely on that one assumption. Second, were the weights re-estimated on a rolling, walk-forward basis, or computed once using the full five years of hindsight and applied retroactively. Third, is the reported 28% an arithmetic average or a properly compounded (geometric) figure, since variance drag at 3x leverage on an equity-like volatility target would meaningfully reduce whatever the arithmetic number is. Fourth, does the backtest account for a realistic execution lag rather than trading on the same closing price used to generate the signal. Any one of these, left unaddressed, can single-handedly explain the gap between a 28% headline and a much more modest realistic outcome.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why does variance drag grow roughly four times larger when portfolio volatility doubles, rather than just doubling along with it?
options: Because transaction costs also double when volatility doubles
Because the variance drag approximation is arithmetic return minus one-half of volatility squared, and squaring a doubled number quadruples it
Because leverage costs scale exponentially with volatility
Because SEBI margin requirements increase nonlinearly with volatility
body.explanation: Variance drag is proportional to volatility squared, not volatility itself. Doubling volatility means squaring a number that has doubled, and (2x)^2 is 4x^2, four times the original squared value, which is exactly why the case study's drag went from 0.98% to 3.92%, almost precisely a fourfold increase, when volatility doubled from 14% to 28%.

body.text: Every one of these mistakes has the same shape: they let a backtest use information, price, cost, or timing, that would not actually have been available in real time, or they quietly skip a real cost. None of them are exotic. They are the default outcome of writing the simplest possible backtesting code, which is exactly why they show up so often. Fixing them is not optional polish, it is the difference between a strategy that worked on paper and a strategy that would have worked in a brokerage account.

points: Look-ahead bias from computing weights once on the full sample and applying them retroactively is the most common risk parity backtesting mistake. The fix is walk-forward, rolling re-estimation at every rebalance date.

Skipping leverage financing costs entirely, or assuming institutional-grade financing a retail investor cannot access, can turn a realistic -5.0% outcome into a reported 24.2% headline, on the exact same portfolio.

Variance drag (geometric return is approximately arithmetic return minus half of volatility squared) grows with the square of volatility, so it matters far more once leverage has scaled volatility up, and it is easy to forget entirely if a backtest reports only arithmetic averages.

Execution timing bias, trading on the same closing price used to generate the signal, assumes instantaneous execution that is not achievable in practice; a one-period lag between signal and trade is the minimum realistic fix.

Selecting a lookback window after seeing which one produced the best backtested performance is a form of overfitting, the estimation-error theme from chapter 1 reappearing in strategy design rather than portfolio construction.

Survivorship bias is mostly avoided by this course's index-level sleeves, but becomes a live risk the moment you backtest factor risk parity on a custom universe of individual stocks rather than a maintained index.
